newsitem.title: CHINA: China smokers, lung cancer deaths see steady rise.
newsitem.headline: China smokers, lung cancer deaths see steady rise.

text.p: The number of smokers in China has steadily grown over the past decade and rising lung cancer deaths may show the habit is taking a deadly toll in the world's most populous nation, a health official said on Thursday.

The proportion of Chinese people who smoked had increased by 3.74 percentage points since 1984 to 37.6 percent at the end of last year, an official of the Chinese Association on Smoking and Health said in a telephone interview.
Lung cancer deaths among the nation's 1.2 billion people had risen an average of 4.5 percent a year since 1990, the official quoted a 1996 survey of nearly 124,000 people as showing.
Some 53.5 percent of non-smokers were exposed to second-hand smoke at least once a week, with 68.3 percent of those inhaling it every day, he said.
He did not give details of health problems associated with second-hand smoke.
The survey found the average Chinese smoker started puffing at age 20, three years younger than in 1984, he said.
The tobacco habit was much more prevalent among males, with 300 million men, or 66.9 percent, smoking compared to just 4.2 percent of women, he said.
China says early deaths, lost productivity and the costs of treating tobacco-related illness cost in 70 billion yuan ($8.4 billion) in 1994, up from 15.9 billion yuan a decade earlier.
Other figures estimate smoking will kill two million people in the year 2025.
China is the world's biggest cigarette market with sales of 1.6 trillion cigarettes a year, and the number of smokers is estimated to be growing by two percent a year, official figures show.
